Battery energy model

Amp-hours converted into watt-hours and runtime

Battery pages need energy context, so this panel connects Ah, voltage, efficiency, Wh, and practical runtime.

Formula Wh = Amps x Volts x Hours

Quick answer

Use this calculator to convert battery capacity into usable energy and runtime context.

Amp-hours only describe current over time. Multiplying by voltage converts capacity into watt-hours, which is easier to compare with appliance and inverter loads.

Wh = Amps x Volts x Hours

Inputs to check before calculating

  • Use the battery nominal voltage for Wh estimates.
  • Apply efficiency loss for inverters, converters, and charging.
  • Check usable capacity limits for lead-acid or lithium batteries.
  • Compare Wh with the actual wattage and runtime of the load.

Example: battery energy estimate

A 100 Ah battery at 120 volts stores about 12,000 watt-hours before efficiency losses. Use the result for runtime planning, then check the battery data sheet for usable capacity limits.

Best use cases

  • Runtime estimates
  • Energy consumption
  • Battery and appliance use
  • single-phase AC load planning with clear unit labels.

Common mistake to avoid

Do not compare amp-hours across different voltages without converting both batteries to watt-hours.

How to use the result

Use Wh and kWh results to compare batteries, estimate runtime, and plan charging needs.

Accuracy and safety note

Calculator output is a planning estimate. Final breaker sizing, wire gauge, derating, voltage-drop limits, equipment protection, and code compliance should be verified with manufacturer documentation and a qualified electrician or engineer.

Amp Power Consumption Calculator uses kWh = A x V x PF x hours / 1,000 to calculate watts, kWh, and energy cost from amps. The tool separates current, voltage, real power, apparent power, and power factor so the result is easier to use for electrical planning.

Use the result for early sizing of circuits, power supplies, solar equipment, generators, LED drivers, speaker amplifiers, and appliance loads. For safety-critical electrical work, verify conductor ampacity, breaker size, derating, and local code requirements before installation.

Methodology, Review Notes, and Sources

How this calculator works

The calculator applies Watt's law for DC and resistive loads, then adds power factor for AC loads and the 1.732 multiplier for balanced three-phase line-to-line calculations.

  • DC and resistive loads: W = A x V
  • Single-phase AC: W = A x V x PF
  • Three-phase AC: W = 1.732 x A x V x PF

FAQ

Power Consumption FAQ

Fast answers before you use the calculator or compare formulas.

Wh How do I convert amp-hours to watt-hours?

Multiply amp-hours by the battery nominal voltage: Wh = Ah × V. A 100Ah battery at 12V stores 1,200 Wh (1.2 kWh). At 24V, the same 100Ah stores 2,400 Wh. This makes comparing batteries at different voltages straightforward.

VS What is the difference between amp-hours and watt-hours?

Amp-hours (Ah) measure charge capacity — how much current a battery can deliver over time. Watt-hours (Wh) measure energy capacity — how much work the stored energy can do. Wh is more useful for comparing batteries because it accounts for voltage. A 50Ah/24V battery (1,200 Wh) stores the same energy as a 100Ah/12V battery (1,200 Wh).

RUN How do I estimate battery runtime from watt-hours?

Divide usable watt-hours by the load in watts: Runtime (hours) = Wh ÷ Watts. A 1,200 Wh battery powering a 100W load lasts approximately 12 hours. For AC loads through an inverter, divide by inverter efficiency (typically 85–92%): 1,200 × 0.90 ÷ 100 = 10.8 hours.

DOD Why can I not use 100% of a battery capacity?

Lead-acid batteries should not be discharged below 50% (only 50% usable). LiFePO4 batteries can safely use 80–90% of rated capacity. AGM batteries are typically limited to 50–60%. Discharging below these limits dramatically shortens battery life. Factor usable capacity into runtime calculations.

CHG How do I calculate charging time from amp-hours?

Divide the amp-hours to replenish by the charging current: Time (hours) = Ah ÷ Charging Amps. A 100Ah battery at 50% SOC needs 50Ah. At 10A charging: 50 ÷ 10 = 5 hours. In practice, add 10–20% for charging efficiency losses, and note that bulk charging slows to absorption/float near full charge.

CMP Can I compare batteries with different voltages using Ah?

No — amp-hours alone do not indicate energy. A 200Ah/6V battery stores 1,200 Wh, while a 50Ah/24V battery also stores 1,200 Wh — identical energy despite very different Ah ratings. Always convert to watt-hours for meaningful comparisons.
